newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: HP plans to boost Asia-Pacific PC sales.
newsitem.headline: HP plans to boost Asia-Pacific PC sales.

text.p: Hewlett-Packard Co said on Thursday it aims to boost personal computer sales in the Asia-Pacific region by 35 percent a year over the next three years.
It was aggressively targeting the portable computing market and wanted to be among the top three players in three years, a top official said.
"Our internal plans for PC business for Asia-Pacific is for growth of 35 percent," Adrian Koch, HP's Asia Pacific general manager of computer products sales and distribution operation, told Reuters.
"The 35 percent (annually) is roughly for a three-year period for all segments, meaning desktop, servers, portables, as an average," he said.
He declined to give HP's Asia-Pacific sales for 1996.

According to research company International Data Corp (IDC), HP's Asia-Pacific shipments, excluding Japan, were 82,500 units in the third quarter of 1996, up 36 percent from the previous year and 7.0 percent higher than the second quarter.
Koch said HP's Asia-Pacific PC business grew more than 60 percent in 1996. IDC said HP shipped 216,966 PCs in 1995.
Koch said the region's PC market was growing at an estimated 20 percent annually into 2000 and HP, with a 35 percent growth target, should be able to increase its market share.
IDC's third-quarter shipment figures show HP in fifth position with a four percent market share.
Koch said HP was attacking the portable computer business after recognising that it had not been a major player in that area.
It aimed to become one of the top three players in the corporate notebook market in the next three years, he told reporters at a briefing.
"One of Hewlett-Packard's primary weaknesses in Asia-Pacific continues to be very low portable volumes," IDC said in a report accompanying its ranking of PC vendors in third quarter of 1996.

"With -9.0 percent sequential growth and -42 percent year-over-year growth, HP's portable difficulties worsened in the third quarter. HP's portable business has been plagued by supply problems, limited channel confidence, and product line vacancies particularly at the low end of the market," it said.
Koch said HP was addressing issues of availability and quality. It can ship its Omnibook portables from its factory in Singapore within four days of receiving an order.

He said HP's new aggression was not a reaction to analyst criticism that it had fared poorly in the portable market, but a reaction to the needs of corporate customers wanting portables to replace existing machines.
Portables made up some 10-12 percent of Asia-Pacific's total PC market, Koch added.
HP's worldwide portable market share was in the one-two percent range, said Andrew Zaremba, HP's worldwide product manager, mobile computing division.
Zaremba said HP could now offer a full range of portables from US$1,900 to more than US$5,000 each, while previously it only catered to the top end of the market.
Koch said he saw portables in Asia-Pacific moving towards 30-35 percent of corporate PCs, similar to current global trend.

John McGilvary, chief analyst at research firm Datapro, told reporters HP's portables had come out top in its 1996 worldwide survey of 2,394 respondents in terms of reputation, reliability, warranty service and overall satisfaction, ahead of IBM, Compaq, Toshiba and Texas Instruments
He said HP's shortcoming was that it was not always the leader in technology and that it did not strongly communicate the strengths of its products to the market place.
